podcast.body: A "ridiculously simple song" recorded in 1968, originally in the key of B flat major but "easily transposable into the key of C." Its melody was later noted for its similarity to The Offspring's "Why Don't You Get A Job," though no public legal action was taken. "1968 Beatles recorded a ridiculously simple song in the key of B flat major, although it's easily transposable into the key of C."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Recorded in 1968, this is a "ridiculously simple song" in the key of B-flat major, though "easily transposable into the key of C." It is widely recognized across Western civilization and shares a strong resemblance to The Offspring's 1999 single "Why Don't You Get A Job." No public legal action was taken, and the similarity was seemingly "treated as some kind of homage." "Pretty much all of Western civilization is familiar with that song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song, released in 1968, is noted for its very basic melody in the key of C, described as something almost any novice could pluck out on a piano. "Very, very basic melody in the key of C. Just about any novice can pluck this one out on a piano."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
